_comment: EXAMPLE · TRIGGERS — WHEN a function runs, which every other examples suite leaves to its descriptor's `triggers` list (tdk fn trigger, fired by hand). A function carrying `trigger_by` is fired by the RUNTIME instead. THE FOUR ANSWERS: nothing (fired by hand, or reactively when a table read with @NEW gets a version — the default); CronTrigger(mask) on a clock, PUBLISHERS ONLY since a publisher has no upstream table to react to; TablesTrigger(tables) when one of a NAMED set produces a batch — which decouples what a function READS from what it WAKES FOR; AllTablesTrigger() when ANY input lands, the blunt instrument that cannot forget a new input. The mask is a five-field UTC cron expression (minute granularity, no seconds) or a descriptor (@hourly, @daily, ...) — Kubernetes CronJob schedules. Paired with Data(df, chunk_size=N), which emits the NEXT N rows per RUN from a per-flow offset: that is what makes a schedule observable, growing the table by 5 rows a minute until the frame is spent and the slot arrives None. The cursor advances per RUN, so a manual trigger consumes a chunk exactly as a tick does. Five functions: trigger_on_cron (every minute + chunked), trigger_on_cron_descriptor (@hourly, fixed frame — versions grow, row count does not), trigger_manually (no trigger_by, the contrast), trigger_on_named_tables (@transformer), trigger_on_any_table (@subscriber into TrashDest, the dev sink that needs no backend). Dev-only. USE --keep: oneshot tears down as soon as the monitor returns, usually before the first tick. One function per file under functions/triggers_scheduling/. Run: `tdx-xp oneshot --suite examples/triggers_scheduling --keep`.
